name: LSQUIC (LiteSpeed QUIC)
workload: HTTP/3 download of an 8GB file over a 10Gbit/s link between two dedicated bare-metal hosts, using an extended QUIC Interop Runner; all client/server pairs across 6 QUIC libraries measured, 50 repetitions per pair.
claimed_speedup: LSQUIC-LSQUIC pair: 3004 Mbit/s vs quiche-quiche pair: 2506 Mbit/s (~1.2x, derived from page data, Fig. 3); with 32x larger UDP receive buffers and architecture-tuned compile flags, LSQUIC*-LSQUIC*: 3882 Mbit/s vs quiche*-quiche*: 2590 Mbit/s (~1.5x, derived from page data, Fig. 10)
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the baseline pairs (example/default builds of each project were used); optimized variants (LSQUIC*/quiche*) used unspecified 'compile flags to optimize for the used architecture' (exact flags not given in the paper text extracted)
hardware: Default: AMD EPYC 7543 (32-core), Broadcom BCM57416 NIC, Debian Bullseye, kernel 5.10.0-8-amd64. Also repeated on AMD EPYC 7551P, Intel Xeon D-1518, Intel Xeon E5-1650, Intel Xeon Gold 6312U (paper Table I).
tradeoffs: Goodput is highly asymmetric by client/server combination: in this same study the quiche-server/LSQUIC-client pair reaches more than 2x the goodput of the LSQUIC-server/quiche-client pair, so the 'LSQUIC beats quiche' result holds for matched same-vendor pairs, not universally across mixed pairs. LSQUIC showed unintended retransmission behavior with BBR congestion control in this study (paper forced Cubic/Reno for all libraries to keep the comparison fair).
caveats: Peer-reviewed (IFIP Networking 2023 / EPIQ lineage, ISBN 978-3-903176-57-7) and the measurement framework + configs + results are published (github.com/tumi8/quic-10g-paper, confirmed the CPU table matches the paper), but the paper text itself does not state the compiler or exact compile flags for the baseline (non-optimized) pairs, so this is capped at Tier B rather than A.
found_via: arXiv API search_query=all:QUIC AND all:implementation AND all:performance -> arxiv.org/abs/2309.16395 'QUIC on the Highway: Evaluating Performance on High-rate Links'

name: quiche-DPDK (tumi8 kernel-bypass fork)
language: C (DPDK kernel-bypass I/O layer added on top of upstream Rust quiche core)
workload: HTTP/3 large-file download between two bare-metal hosts using an extended QUIC Interop Runner framework; vanilla kernel-socket quiche-quiche pair vs DPDK-kernel-bypass quiche-dpdk-quiche-dpdk pair, 50 repetitions each.
claimed_speedup: ~1.83x goodput: quiche-quiche (kernel) pair averaged 3241 Mbit/s vs quiche-dpdk-quiche-dpdk pair averaging 5937 Mbit/s (derived from page data: measurement-data/01-implementation-matrix/processed.csv)
hardware: Bare-metal server pair; NIC using the Intel 'ice' driver (E810 family) per framework/testbed/testbed_stoi-pact.json. Exact CPU model not found in the repository content inspected this session (paper not yet formally published: DOI listed as TODO, venue NOMS 2026).
stars_or_usage: 0 stars (research artifact accompanying a NOMS 2026 paper)
tradeoffs: DPDK requires dedicating a whole NIC/queue to userspace polling (no shared use with the kernel network stack), hugepages, and root/elevated privileges; adds substantial deployment complexity vs a drop-in library. No license file found in this repo (upstream quiche is Apache-2.0/BSD-2-Clause), so treat the fork's own additions as 'look but don't copy' pending clarification from the authors.
caveats: Numbers are derived directly from the research group's own published raw CSV (dataset mirrored on Zenodo, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.18630971), not from the camera-ready paper text (README lists the paper DOI as TODO; presented at NOMS 2026). CPU model and exact compiler flags were not found in the parts of the repo inspected this session. The same group's prior, closely related methodology (QUIC on the Highway) was peer-reviewed at IFIP Networking 2023.
found_via: gh api orgs/tumi8/repos (listing) -> tumi8/quiche-dpdk README pointing to paper 'Kernel Bypass Surgery: A Viable Procedure for Maximizing QUIC Bandwidth?' -> gh api repos/tumi8/quic-bypass-paper and its measurement-data CSVs

name: LSQUIC-DPDK (tumi8 kernel-bypass fork)
workload: HTTP/3 large-file download between two bare-metal hosts, DPDK+SR-IOV kernel-bypass builds of each QUIC library, same-implementation client/server pairs, 50 repetitions each (measurement-data/06-dpdk-integration).
claimed_speedup: LSQUIC-DPDK (SR-IOV) pair averaged 11019 Mbit/s vs MsQuic-DPDK (SR-IOV) pair averaging 8118 Mbit/s (~1.36x); also beats quiche-DPDK (SR-IOV) pair averaging 6168 Mbit/s (~1.79x) in the same table (derived from page data)
hardware: Bare-metal server pair; NIC using the Intel 'ice' driver (E810 family) with SR-IOV. Exact CPU model not found in the repository content inspected this session.
stars_or_usage: 0 stars (research artifact accompanying a NOMS 2026 paper)
tradeoffs: Same DPDK/SR-IOV deployment complexity as other entries in this family (dedicated NIC/queue, hugepages, root). A separate table in the same dataset (measurement-data/01-implementation-matrix/processed.csv) shows msquic-dpdk NOT beating vanilla kernel msquic (7982 vs 8250 Mbit/s), so DPDK's benefit is very implementation-dependent; only the head-to-head DPDK-vs-DPDK cross-library comparison used here is a clean win for LSQUIC-DPDK.
caveats: Same unpublished-paper caveat as the quiche-DPDK entry above (DOI TODO, NOMS 2026); numbers come straight from the group's published CSV rather than paper prose. Treat the ratio as directional given some inconsistency between the two published data tables for msquic-dpdk.
found_via: Same discovery path as quiche-DPDK entry: gh api orgs/tumi8/repos -> tumi8/quic-bypass-paper -> measurement-data/06-dpdk-integration/processed.csv

name: picoquic-DPDK (Tyunyayev kernel-bypass fork)
workload: DPDK kernel-bypass QUIC I/O vs standard kernel-socket picoquic; exact workload (file size, link rate) not confirmed since the primary paper text could not be accessed (ACM DL page returned 403; no arXiv or accessible preprint found).
claimed_speedup: "increased the throughput by a factor of three" - as paraphrased in a later, unrelated peer-reviewed paper's related-work section, not the original source
tradeoffs: DPDK kernel bypass requires a dedicated NIC/queue, hugepages, and root; README describes the project as 'work in progress'. A companion experiments repo (UCLouvain-ENSG/picoquic-dpdk-experiments) is explicitly set up to compare it against quicly, quiche, and msquic directly, but the specific numeric results for those comparisons could not be retrieved this session.
caveats: The '3x' figure is a secondhand paraphrase from arXiv:2309.16395's related-work section describing Tyunyayev et al., 'A High-Speed QUIC Implementation' (CoNEXT-SW 2022), not the primary source (dl.acm.org and the UCLouvain lab page both returned 403 this session; no arXiv/DBLP-accessible copy found, and Semantic Scholar was rate-limited throughout this run). It is unclear whether the 3x baseline is plain picoquic (most likely, given typical DPDK-paper structure) or one of the named incumbents its companion experiments repo also targets (quiche/msquic). Confidence lowered accordingly.
